description: Single-panel table (Table 2, "Mechanical properties of the experimental steel samples") rendered as an image, with a horizontal rule separating the header row from two data rows; no other panels, axes, scale bars or images are present. The header lists six columns exactly as printed: "Steel", "YS [MPa]", "UTS [MPa]", "RA [%]", "A [%]" and "CVN [J]". The two data rows are the two nitrogen conditions of the Fe-28Mn-10Al-0.8C low-density steel: "LN" (low nitrogen) and "HN" (high nitrogen), each with a ± uncertainty in parentheses. LN gives YS 685(±1.5) MPa, UTS 832.5(±1.5) MPa, RA 57(±6) %, A 62.5(±5) % and CVN 81(±3) J; HN gives YS 647(±1) MPa, UTS 841.5(±3.5) MPa, RA 70(±2) %, A 74.5(±2.5) % and CVN 130.5(±5.5) J. Read across the rows, the table shows that nitrogen addition raises UTS slightly (by 9 MPa), raises RA by 13 percentage points, A by 12 percentage points and CVN by 49.5 J, while lowering YS by 38 MPa. The table thus supplies the quantitative strength, ductility and impact-toughness basis for the paper's claim that nitrogen enhances tensile strength, plasticity and impact toughness but reduces yield strength. No microstructural or curve data are shown.

observations.observation: The table's column headers are printed as Steel, YS [MPa], UTS [MPa], RA [%], A [%] and CVN [J].
The table contains exactly two data rows, labelled LN and HN, one per nitrogen condition of the experimental steel.
For LN the printed values are YS 685(±1.5) MPa, UTS 832.5(±1.5) MPa, RA 57(±6) %, A 62.5(±5) % and CVN 81(±3) J.
For HN the printed values are YS 647(±1) MPa, UTS 841.5(±3.5) MPa, RA 70(±2) %, A 74.5(±2.5) % and CVN 130.5(±5.5) J.
UTS is higher for HN (841.5 MPa) than for LN (832.5 MPa), a difference of 9 MPa.
YS is lower for HN (647 MPa) than for LN (685 MPa), a difference of 38 MPa.
RA and A are higher for HN (70% and 74.5%) than for LN (57% and 62.5%), i.e. 13 and 12 percentage points higher respectively.
CVN impact energy is 130.5 J for HN versus 81 J for LN, a difference of 49.5 J.
The citing text states that the UTS values for the low-nitrogen (LN) and high-nitrogen (HN) steels were 832.5 and 841.5 MPa, respectively.
The citing text states that the RA and A values for the HN steel were 13% and 12% higher than those of the LN steel, and that the impact energy of the HN steel was 49.5 J higher.
The citing text states that with the addition of nitrogen the UTS, plasticity and impact toughness were enhanced while the YS was reduced.
The citing text attributes the slightly lower YS of the HN steel to its lower ferrite content, quoting ferrite area percentages of 5.08% for LN and 1.84% for HN (see Figure 3).
The caption identifies the table as Table 2, Mechanical properties of the experimental steel samples. No sample values beyond the two rows are given.
